description: Schedules, work, and the school run. Six verbs that run a day (have, want, know, can, say, give), telling time, and ten more letters.
objectives: Ask and tell the time, and talk about today, this week, work, and pickups.
Conjugate six new verbs (have, want, know, can, say, give) in present and past, with negatives, and say what’s happening right now (dāram miram).
Hear gh against g, catch the glottal stop, and recognize how this week’s verbs shrink in speech.
Read and write 10 more letters (ز ذ ژ ج چ ح خ س ش م): 21 in all, including every letter that never joins forward.
Add eight phrases to the gossip kit, and play “Sā’at chande, āghā gorge?” with the girls.

words.root: From Arabic. Vaght dāri? is “do you have time?”, and vaght-e shām is dinner time.
Spelled exactly like ki (who?): کی. Only the vowel and the context tell them apart. Key miyāy? When are you coming? Ki miyād? Who’s coming?
Clock times add -o nim, “and a half”: haft-o nim is 7:30. A nimru (half-face) is a fried egg, sunny side up.
Arabic for one fourth. Listen for the catch at the end: rob’. Se-o rob’ is 3:15.

example.en: Wait a quarter of an hour.

words.root: Also the name of the noon prayer. Ba’d az zohr, “after noon,” is the afternoon, the same idea as English.

example.en: Are you coming home at noon?

words.root: From haft, seven: a seven-ness. Careful: sā’at hafte means “it’s seven o’clock” (haft + -e, is). Same sound, different words.

example.en: I have a lot of work this week.

words.root: Literally “at the head of the work.” Sar (head) is everywhere: hamsar, and saram sholughe, “my head is crowded,” I’m swamped.
From the Arabic for “to sit”: a sitting.

example.en: I have a meeting at ten.

words.root: The -an ending, written with a little double stroke over the alef (ـاً), makes adverbs out of Arabic words: ma’mulan (usually), ba’dan (later), masalan (for example).

example.en: I usually come home at six.

words.root: hich (none) + vaght (time): no-time. Persian doubles the negative: hichvaght nemiyād, literally “he no-time doesn’t come,” is “he never comes.”

example.en: He’s never late. (he never comes late)

words.en: well done; welcome back (to someone who’s been working)
words.root: Literally “may you not be tired.” You say it to anyone who has been working: at the door after work, to a cashier, to a plumber. The answer is salāmat bāshi, “may you be well.”

example.en: Well done today! Thanks, you too.

words.root: From the Arabic for “to study”: the place of study. The same root gives dars, a lesson.
Literally “the tail end, following.” Miram donbāl-e bachchehā, “I’m going after the kids,” is how Persian says I’ll pick up the kids.

example.en: I’m going to pick up the kids.

words.root: From French machine. In Persian, the machine is the car.
Tehran’s traffic is legendary, so this word gets a lot of use. Persian doesn’t start a syllable with two consonants, so tr gets an e: te-rāfik.
se (three) + shanbe (Saturday): the third day after Saturday. The whole system is Day 5’s word story.

example.en: I have a meeting on Tuesday.

words.root: panj (five) + shanbe. In Iran the weekend is Thursday and Friday, so Thursday night is the big night out.
The word also means chameleon, or anything that changes color. The turkey got it for its wattles, which flush red, blue, and white.
Harf zadan, “to strike words,” is to talk. Harf-e mardom, people’s talk, is gossip. And every letter you’re learning is a harf.

days.subtitle: Want and have: the two verbs that plan a day
days.objective: Tell the time, say what you want and what you have on today, and read روز (day).

steps.title: Warm-up: what do you remember?
steps.instruction: A new chapter, the same habit: pull old words out of memory first.

steps.title: Listen first
steps.instruction: Monday morning. Sam has lost track of time. Play the scene twice before you look at the words, then tap a line to reveal its English.

lines.fa: نه، وقت داری. یه ربع وقت داری.
lines.tr: na, vaght dāri. ye rob’ vaght dāri.
lines.en: No, you have time. You have a quarter of an hour.
lines.speaker: Mass

lines.en: Today at noon I’m busy. (I have work)
lines.speaker: Sam

steps.title: New words
steps.instruction: Six words for the clock and the calendar. Tap each one, say it out loud, and read its story.

steps.title: Verb lab: want and have
steps.intro: The present, in depth. One form covers three English tenses: mikhām is I want, I’m wanting, and, with a time word, I’ll want. The mark is mi-, and the stress lands on it: MI-khām. Two everyday verbs break the rule. budan hides inside its endings (khubam), and dāshtan never takes mi-: dāram, I have. Dāshtan is how Persian plans a day: vaght dāram (I have time), kār dāram (I’m busy, literally “I have work”), jalase dāram (I have a meeting). Leave the dust dāshtan tab for Day 4.

steps.title: Ear gym: gh or g?
steps.instruction: Persian gh (written ق or غ; Tehranis say them the same) is made farther back than g, where you gargle. English has nothing like it, so your ear keeps filing it under g. Play each pair until the gh sounds rough and the g sounds clean, then take the test.

steps.title: Reading: ز ذ ژ

letters.name: ze
letters.tip: Re with a dot on top: the same short slide below the line, and like re it never joins forward.

letters.name: zāl
letters.tip: Dāl with a dot. In Arabic it’s the th of “this”; Persian says plain z. It’s rare. Recognize it, don’t sweat it.

letters.name: zhe
letters.tip: Re with three dots. Arabic has no zh, so Persian added dots to make one, the way it did for p. With ژ you’ve met all seven letters that never join forward: ا د ذ ر ز ژ و.

steps.intro: Week two of the alphabet. You already own the shapes. These three are re and dāl wearing dots, so the only new thing to learn is where the dots go. All three refuse to join forward, like their parents.
steps.aside: Roz, the English name, is Persian ruz, day. So is Nowruz, the Persian New Year: now (new) + ruz (day). You can read روز now; you’ll be able to read نوروز in two weeks.

steps.title: Shadow the scene
steps.instruction: Play a line, then say it on top of the voice. Lean on mi-: shām MI-khāy? Record yourself and compare.

lines.fa: نه، وقت داری. یه ربع وقت داری.
lines.tr: na, vaght dāri. ye rob’ vaght dāri.
lines.en: No, you have time. You have a quarter of an hour.
lines.speaker: Mass

questions.prompt: Mass asks “key miyāy khune?” What does she want to know?
questions.explain: key (when) and ki (who) are both spelled کی. Your ear tells them apart, not your eye.

questions.prompt: How do you say “I’m busy” (I have work)?
questions.explain: dāshtan never takes mi- in the present.

questions.prompt: Type what you hear, in English letters.

steps.title: In your notebook
tasks: Write ز, ذ, and ژ five times each, saying the sound every time. Then write all seven letters that never join forward in one row: ا د ذ ر ز ژ و.
Write روز, زود, ذرت, and ژاپن three times each, with phonetics and meaning underneath.
Draw a clock face. Around it, write the hours in phonetics: sā’at-e yek… sā’at-e davāzdah. Under it, write haft-o nim and se-o rob’.
Copy the present of khāstan from the verb lab. Cover it and write it again from memory.
Add khāstan and dāshtan to “Verbs I own,” with both stems. Note beside dāshtan: no mi-.

steps.title: Talk with Mass

openers.en: What do you have on today?

steps.massNote: Sam is learning to tell time. Ask him the time whenever you think of it, and make him answer in Farsi: “haft-o nim,” “se-o rob’.”

steps.title: Teach the girls: Sā’at chande, āghā gorge?
steps.game: “What’s the time, Mr. Wolf?” in Persian. You’re the wolf (gorg), back turned. The girls call “sā’at chande, āghā gorge?” and you answer an hour; they take that many steps toward you, counting out loud in Farsi. When you shout “vaght-e shāme!” (dinner time!), turn and chase. Whoever gets caught is the next wolf, and has to answer in Farsi.

items.en: What time is it, Mr. Wolf?

days.subtitle: Know and can, and the two most useful “no”s
days.objective: Talk about work and meetings, say what you know and what you can do, hear the glottal stop, and read چای and خواب.

steps.title: Warm-up: what do you remember?
steps.instruction: Yesterday’s words and some old friends from Mango.

steps.title: Listen first
steps.instruction: Evening. Sam comes home from work. Listen twice, then tap lines for the English.

lines.en: Welcome home! (may you not be tired)
lines.speaker: Mass

lines.en: Thanks. I was swamped. (my head was very crowded)
lines.speaker: Sam

lines.fa: آره، سه تا. معمولاً یکی دارم.
lines.tr: āre, se tā. ma’mulan yeki dāram.
lines.en: Yes, three. Usually I have one.
lines.speaker: Sam

lines.en: Are you coming home at noon tomorrow?
lines.speaker: Mass

lines.fa: نه، نمی‌تونم. فردا هم جلسه دارم.
lines.tr: na, nemitunam. fardā ham jalase dāram.
lines.en: No, I can’t. I have a meeting tomorrow too.
lines.speaker: Sam

steps.title: New words
steps.instruction: Five words for the working day, including the greeting every Iranian worker hears.

steps.title: Verb lab: know and can
steps.intro: dunestan (know) and tunestan (can) are near twins. Both lose a syllable in speech, and their forms rhyme all the way down: midunam, mitunam. Their negatives may be the most useful words this week: nemidunam (I don’t know) and nemitunam (I can’t). The negative of any mi- verb is ne-mi-, and the stress jumps forward to ne-: NE-midunam. Neither verb has an everyday command.

steps.title: Ear gym: the glottal stop
steps.instruction: The apostrophe in ba’d, sā’at, and rob’ is a glottal stop: the tiny catch in the middle of “uh-oh.” It’s written with ع or ء, letters you’ll meet next week. In fast Tehrani speech the catch often melts into a longer vowel, so ba’d can sound almost like bād (wind). Listen for the catch.

steps.title: Reading: ج چ ح خ

letters.name: jim
letters.tip: A cup with a tail and one dot inside. At the start or in the middle of a word the tail drops off and only the hook is left.

letters.name: che
letters.tip: The same cup with three dots: another Persian addition (p, ch, zh, and next week g). Now you can write chāy.

letters.name: he
letters.tip: The cup with no dots. One of two letters for h; this one comes in words from Arabic, like hāl and hosele. Say it as plain breath.

letters.name: khe
letters.tip: The cup with one dot on top. Watch for خوا: when kh is followed by وا, the و is silent. خواب is khāb. It’s why khāstan (want) is spelled خواستن.

steps.intro: One body, four letters. The cup-with-a-tail shape is the same in all of them; the dots do the work: one inside for j, three inside for ch, none for h, one on top for kh. Learn the body once and the dots are just labels.
steps.aside: You can now read the word on every Persian tea glass: چای. And خواب has a ghost in it: the و is silent, a leftover from how the word was said a thousand years ago.

steps.title: Shadow the scene
steps.instruction: Copy the tune of “khaste nabāshi”: it falls at the end, like a kind word, not a question. In nemitunam, lean on ne-.

lines.en: Welcome home! (may you not be tired)
lines.speaker: Mass

lines.fa: آره، سه تا. معمولاً یکی دارم.
lines.tr: āre, se tā. ma’mulan yeki dāram.
lines.en: Yes, three. Usually I have one.
lines.speaker: Sam

lines.fa: نه، نمی‌تونم. فردا هم جلسه دارم.
lines.tr: na, nemitunam. fardā ham jalase dāram.
lines.en: No, I can’t. I have a meeting tomorrow too.
lines.speaker: Sam

questions.prompt: How do you say “He’s never late”?
questions.explain: Persian doubles the negative: “never” plus “doesn’t come.”

steps.title: In your notebook
tasks: Write ج, چ, ح, and خ in all four shapes. The body never changes; say the sound as you add the dots.
Write چای, برنج, خوب, and خواب with phonetics and meaning. Under خواب, write: the و is silent.
Write tomorrow’s real schedule in phonetics: sā’at-e hasht…, zohr…, sā’at-e shish… Use ma’mulan or hichvaght at least once.
Write two tables side by side, all six persons: midunam / nemidunam and mitunam / nemitunam.
Add dunestan and tunestan to “Verbs I own.”

steps.title: Talk with Mass
steps.massNote: When Sam finishes work, greet him with “khaste nabāshi!” He should answer “salāmat bāshi.” Then ask about his day.

days.subtitle: Say and give, and how verbs shrink in Mass’s mouth
days.objective: Follow a phone call from the car, tell and give, hear written verbs shrink into spoken ones, and read امروز and شام. That makes 21 letters.

steps.title: Warm-up: what do you remember?
steps.instruction: Retrieval first, always.

steps.title: Listen first
steps.instruction: A phone call at 2:45. Sam is stuck in traffic. Listen twice before reading.

lines.en: I’m in the car. There’s traffic!
lines.speaker: Sam

lines.en: Are you picking up the kids?
lines.speaker: Mass

lines.fa: آره. مدرسه ساعت سه تعطیل می‌شه؟
lines.tr: āre. madrese sā’at-e se ta’til mishe?
lines.en: Yes. School gets out at three?
lines.speaker: Sam

lines.en: Tell the kids dinner is macaroni!
lines.speaker: Mass

steps.title: New words
steps.instruction: Four words for the school run.

steps.title: Verb lab: say and give
steps.intro: goftan (say) and dādan (give) both have written present stems that speech crushes: gu- becomes g-, dah- becomes d-. That leaves pairs one sound apart: mige (says) and mide (gives). Commands are back: begu! (tell me!), nagu! (don’t tell!), bede! (give it!), nade! (don’t give it!). Leave the gush dādan tab for Day 4.

steps.title: Ear gym: written vs. spoken, part 2
steps.instruction: Last week: ān becomes un, and -ad becomes -e. This week’s verbs lose whole chunks, and “is” shrinks to a single sound. Learn both columns: the left is what you’ll read, the right is what you’ll hear.

rules.name: stems shrink
rules.text: In speech, the middle of the present stem drops out: khāh → khā, dān → dun, tavān → tun, guy → g, dah → d.

rules.name: ast → -e
rules.text: “Is” (ast) becomes an -e stuck to the end of the word, or -st after a vowel.

steps.title: Reading: س ش م

letters.name: sin
letters.tip: Three little teeth on the line, then a bowl at the end of a word. Joined up, it’s just the row of teeth.

letters.name: shin
letters.tip: The same teeth with three dots on top. Three dots over teeth is sh.

letters.name: mim
letters.tip: A small loop. At the end of a word it drops a tail straight down. You’ll write it constantly: it’s the -am of every “I” verb.

steps.intro: Teeth and a loop. Sin and shin are the same row of teeth; three dots make it sh. Mim is the last letter of the week, and the one you’ll write most, because every “I” verb ends in it: midunam, mikhām, dāram.
steps.aside: With mim you can read the endings of every verb you know. Try دارم (dāram), می‌خوام (mikhām), and نمی‌دونم (nemidunam): every letter in them is yours.

steps.title: Shadow the scene
steps.instruction: Stress lives on mi-: MI-ri, MI-gam. In a negative it jumps to ne-: NE-migam. Match where Mass leans, then record.

questions.prompt: Mass says “sā’at hafte.” What does she mean?
questions.explain: haft (seven) + -e (is). It sounds exactly like hafte, week. Context decides.

questions.prompt: Type what you hear, in English letters.

steps.title: In your notebook
tasks: Write س, ش, and م five times each. Then write all 21 letters you know, from memory, and check.
Write شب, سیب, شام, امروز, and می‌دونم with phonetics and meaning.
Write the five written → spoken verb pairs from the ear gym (mikhāham → mikhām…). Say each spoken one with the stress on mi-.
Write five things you say to the kids, in phonetics, using begu, nagu, bede, and nade.

steps.title: Talk with Mass
steps.massNote: Sam is learning say and give. At dinner, ask him for things in Farsi (“nun-o bede,” pass the bread) and make him tell you things (“begu!”).

days.subtitle: Story day: right now (dāram miram), gossip kit part 2, and Khayyam on time
days.objective: Follow the second story, say what’s happening right now, gossip with dunestan and goftan, and read a quatrain of Khayyam with a word-by-word key.

steps.title: Warm-up: what do you remember?
steps.instruction: Mixed: this week and older words.

steps.title: Story, episode 2: The turkey
steps.instruction: Thanksgiving. The lazy neighbor from episode 1 is up to something. Listen to the whole episode before reading, then read along line by line.

lines.fa: پنج‌شنبه‌ست. سام و معصومه دوباره پشت پنجره‌ان.
lines.tr: panjshanbe-st. sām-o ma’sume dobāre posht-e panjere-an.
lines.en: It’s Thursday. Sam and Massoumeh are at the window again.

lines.fa: نمی‌دونم. ولی اون هیچ‌وقت مهمون نداره!

lines.en: I don’t know. But he never has guests!
lines.speaker: Mass

steps.title: New words
steps.instruction: Two days of the week, the bird of the day, and the word for talk.

steps.title: Verb lab: right now, and two compounds
steps.intro: Right now. The plain present already means “I go, I’m going, I’ll go.” When you need “I’m in the middle of it,” put dāshtan in front, conjugated for the same person: dāram miram (I’m on my way), dāre miyād (he’s coming), dārim mikhorim (we’re eating). Both halves change with the person. This form has no negative: for “I’m not going,” just say nemiram. Two compounds. Open the tabs: dust (friend) + dāshtan = like or love, and gush (ear) + dādan = listen. As with sabr kardan, only the verb changes.

quiz.explain: The “right now” form has no negative. Use the plain present.
Both halves agree with “they”: dāran + miyān.

steps.title: Gossip kit, part 2
steps.intro: Part 1 was for pointing. Part 2 is for the news itself: who knows, who’s telling, and who might be listening.

proverb.fa: زبان سرخ سر سبز می‌دهد بر باد
proverb.tr: zabān-e sorkh sar-e sabz midahad bar bād
proverb.en: The red tongue gives the green head to the wind. (Loose talk costs heads.)

steps.tip: When the person you’re talking about walks in, switch topics without a pause. Ask loudly: “shām chi dārim?” (What’s for dinner?)

steps.title: Khayyam on time

lines.en: This caravan of life passes strangely.

lines.fa: دریاب دمی که با طرب می‌گذرد
lines.tr: daryāb dami ke bā tarab migozarad
lines.en: Seize a moment that passes in joy.

steps.note: Khayyam was an astronomer before he was a poet. He helped reform the Persian solar calendar, famously accurate and still in use, so this is a poem about time from a man who measured it. Dam means breath, and a moment is one breath long. The quatrain ends: “Cupbearer, why grieve over tomorrow? Bring the cup: the night is passing.”

steps.title: Word stories: the -gāh family
steps.intro: -gāh turns a noun or a verb stem into the place where it happens. It also means time: gāhi is “sometimes.” Place and time in one syllable.

items.story: The place of knowing. The dān is the same as in midunam.
The place of sleep, with the silent vāv you met on Day 2.

questions.prompt: How do you say “He’s coming” (right now)?

steps.title: Word stories: the days of the week
steps.intro: Shanbe, from the same root as Sabbath, anchors the Persian week. After it, the days are just a count: one-shanbe, two-shanbe, up to five. Then Friday, jome, breaks the pattern. In fast speech the n slides toward m before b: shambe, yekshambe.

items.story: Four after Saturday. Chāharshanbe Suri, the fire-jumping night before Nowruz, is held on the eve of the year’s last Wednesday.
Five after Saturday, and the start of the Iranian weekend.
The day of gathering, for Friday prayers. The pattern breaks for the day of rest.
